prompt.context_jp: 朝の光がオフィス街を染める頃、鶸田は五十社目にしてやっと得たこの職場へ足を向けていた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 朝の光___オフィス街を染める頃、鶸田は…
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle that introduces the scene-setting image.

feedback.correct_en: This opening line sets a fresh visual scene — the morning light is new information being painted into view, so が is natural. は would wrongly treat 朝の光 as a known topic already under discussion.
feedback.incorrect_en: は here would sound like 'as for the morning light…', suggesting it was already the topic, but the sentence is introducing the imagery for the first time.

contrast_examples.en: As for the rain, it has stopped. (known topic)

prompt.context_jp: 朝の光がオフィス街を染める頃、鶸田は五十社目にしてやっと得たこの職場へ足を向けていた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 鶸田___五十社目にしてやっと得たこの職場へ足を向けていた。
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the particle marking the sentence's main topic.

feedback.correct_en: Hiwada is the ongoing protagonist whose actions the narrator wants to describe — classic topic は. が would make it sound like we're identifying who (of several candidates) went, which doesn't match the narrative stance.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would suggest exhaustive identification ('it was Hiwada who…'), but the sentence is simply narrating what the already-known main character is doing.

contrast_examples.en: He is the one who went. (identifying)

prompt.context_jp: 鷹野は前から歩いてきたサラリーマンと正面からぶつかってしまった。
prompt.prompt_jp: 相手のカフェラテ___宙を舞い、鷹野の白いブラウスにも、相手のスーツにも大きなしみが広がっていく。
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the particle that reports the sudden event.

feedback.correct_en: The latte flying up is a new, dramatic event the narrator introduces — が. は would wrongly imply the latte was already being discussed as a topic.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would frame the latte as the ongoing topic, but this sentence is a surprise moment captured as it happens.

prompt.context_jp: 見ているうちに、鷹野は前から歩いてきたサラリーマンと正面からぶつかってしまった。
prompt.prompt_jp: 鷹野___前から歩いてきたサラリーマンと正面からぶつかってしまった。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle for Takano as the ongoing topic.

feedback.correct_en: Takano is the already-established topic Hiwada has been watching. は keeps her as the frame; が would single her out as newly identified.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would feel like 'it was Takano (of all people) who collided', but the paragraph has been tracking her all along.

prompt.context_jp: 鳩山がしみ抜きの手順を教え始める場面。
prompt.prompt_jp: カフェラテ___ミルクを含んでるから油溶性なんだ。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle that announces the topic of explanation.

feedback.correct_en: Hatoyama is launching into an explanation about café latte as a general topic ('as for café latte…'). は is the natural 'topic for explanation' marker; が would make it sound like identifying which drink contains milk.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would single out latte as the one that happens to contain milk, but Hatoyama is giving a general lesson about the drink itself.

prompt.context_jp: 鳩山が「クリーニング代請求すりゃよかったのに」と言ったのに対して。
prompt.prompt_jp: 鷹野___大丈夫だって…
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the particle that reports what Takano said (subordinate clause subject).

feedback.correct_en: Inside a 「〜って」 reported clause, Takano is the embedded subject providing new information — が is standard. は would try to make her the main topic of the whole utterance, which doesn't fit this embedded structure.
feedback.incorrect_en: は in an embedded quote clause tends to feel like a contrast or extracted topic; here Hiwada is simply reporting that Takano said she was fine.

contrast_examples.en: He said he would come. (embedded subject)
As for him, he said he would come. (topicalized)

prompt.context_jp: 鷹野にしみ抜きの事情を伝える場面。
prompt.prompt_jp: 鷹野、鳩山さん___一生懸命 落としてくれたんだよ。
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the particle that highlights who did the work.

feedback.correct_en: The speaker is spotlighting that it was Hatoyama specifically who put in the effort — this exhaustive/identifying nuance calls for が. は would downshift it to 'as for Hatoyama', losing the appreciative emphasis.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would turn the sentence into a neutral comment about Hatoyama, but Hiwada is urging Takano to recognize the person who worked hard for her.

contrast_examples.jp: 母が作ってくれたんだよ。
contrast_examples.en: It was Mom who made it for you. (identifying the doer)
Mom is good at cooking. (topic comment)

prompt.context_jp: 鳩山が鷹野のパソコンを見に行った場面。
prompt.prompt_jp: ブラウザの接続___タイムアウトしていた、というごく単純なものだった。
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the particle that reveals the cause for the first time.

feedback.correct_en: The sentence delivers newly discovered information — the browser connection had timed out. New-info が fits. は would presuppose we were already talking about the browser connection as a topic.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would mislead the reader into expecting a contrast ('the browser connection, (unlike something), had timed out'); the narrative just reveals the simple cause.

prompt.context_jp: 数日後の営業部でのこと。
prompt.prompt_jp: 鵜飼___突然、鷹野を営業の同行者として指名する事件が起きた。
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the particle that introduces who did the unexpected thing.

feedback.correct_en: This clause introduces a new event with Ukai as the surprising actor — new-information が. Because Ukai was not the previous topic and the whole sentence reports a 事件, が is natural.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would frame Ukai as a continuing topic, but she is being spotlighted here as the unexpected source of the incident.

contrast_examples.en: The manager is a strict person. (topic)

prompt.context_jp: 株式会社FREEDOM MODEについての説明。
prompt.prompt_jp: 社長___若い頃から業界の反逆児と呼ばれていた。
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the particle marking the sentence topic.

feedback.correct_en: The sentence makes a general characterization of the CEO — classic 'A は B だ' topic-comment structure. は presents the CEO as the subject of discussion.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would make it feel like identifying 'which person was called the industry rebel', but we already know we're talking about this specific CEO.

prompt.context_jp: FREEDOM MODEの社風を説明する雉谷。
prompt.prompt_jp: 最近 この会社の営業___ スーツもジャケットも 着ないんだって。
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the particle that frames 'the sales team at this company (as opposed to others)'.

feedback.correct_en: The sentence contrasts THIS company's sales team against the norm — は carries that contrastive 'as for them' flavor. が would wrongly introduce them as new specific actors doing something.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would spotlight them as the agents of an event; here, the point is a general policy that distinguishes them from other companies.

contrast_examples.jp: ウチの会社はスーツを着ない。
contrast_examples.en: At our company we don't wear suits. (contrast with norm)

contrast_examples.jp: 田中さんがスーツを着ていない。
contrast_examples.en: Tanaka isn't wearing a suit. (specific observation)

prompt.context_jp: 鵙尾が自作のシステムを見せる場面。
prompt.prompt_jp: これ… あたし___作った 経費精算システムなんだけど。
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the particle inside the relative clause.

feedback.correct_en: Inside a noun-modifying (relative) clause like 'the system I made', the embedded subject takes が, not は. は is largely blocked from relative clauses.
feedback.incorrect_en: は inside this relative clause would sound wrong — は tends to be reserved for main-clause topics, not embedded modifiers.

contrast_examples.en: As for me, I wrote a book. (main clause topic)

prompt.context_jp: 鵜飼が鵙尾に抗議する場面。
prompt.prompt_jp: ウチの鷹野の 大事な勤務時間___ 他部署の方に使われると 困るんですけど。
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the particle marking what is being used.

feedback.correct_en: In a passive like 使われる, the thing acted on is still marked with を when the agent is marked with に ('X を Y に使われる' = 'to have X used by Y'). Here, Takano's work hours are what's being used.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would mark the subject of a direct-passive, which doesn't fit this adversative construction. に marks the agent (他部署の方), not the thing used.

contrast_examples.en: I had my wallet taken by someone.

prompt.context_jp: 朱雀が過去を語る場面。
prompt.prompt_jp: ある日の飲み会___、朱雀はまた鵜飼の恋愛の失敗を茶化していた。
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the particle marking where the event took place.

feedback.correct_en: で marks the location of an action — the teasing happened AT a drinking party. に would mark a point/destination, not the venue of an activity.
feedback.incorrect_en: に with a time-like noun would suggest a point in time but not frame it as the setting of ongoing teasing. を would wrongly turn the party into a direct object.

contrast_examples.en: I talked at a café. (location of action)

prompt.context_jp: 鷹野が早退するときの一言。
prompt.prompt_jp: すみません コイのため___ 行かなくてはならなくて 失礼します。
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the particle expressing 'for the sake of'.

feedback.correct_en: 〜のために is a set phrase meaning 'for the sake of' and takes に inside it. で would mark a means or location, not purpose.
feedback.incorrect_en: で would wrongly treat コイのため as a means or location. を doesn't fit after ため at all.

prompt.context_jp: 鷹野がぶつかった相手を怒らせずに済ませたのを見た鶸田。
prompt.prompt_jp: なんて___が広い人なんだ… あんな大人になりたい。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the word that fits the idiom for 'tolerant/forgiving person'.

feedback.correct_en: 心が広い is the set phrase for 'broad-minded / forgiving'. The other body parts form different idioms with different meanings.
feedback.incorrect_en: 手が広い means 'has wide connections'; 顔が広い means 'well-known / well-connected'. Neither captures the forgiving-toward-the-collision nuance here.

contrast_examples.en: He knows a lot of people.

prompt.context_jp: 教育係にしみ抜きをさせても気にしない鷹野の様子を見た鶸田。
prompt.prompt_jp: 自分の教育係に しみ抜きをさせても 意に介さない ___ あれは わざとなのか？
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the noun for 'brazen/shameless unflappability'.

feedback.correct_en: ふてぶてしさ captures the audacious, unapologetic nerve Hiwada senses in Takano. やさしさ (kindness) and まじめさ (seriousness) are positively valenced and don't match his suspicious judgment.
feedback.incorrect_en: やさしさ or まじめさ would reverse the critical tone — Hiwada is suggesting she might be deliberately shameless, not kind or earnest.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼のふてぶてしさに驚いた。
contrast_examples.en: I was surprised by his audacity.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼のやさしさに感動した。
contrast_examples.en: I was moved by his kindness.

prompt.context_jp: ブラウザがタイムアウトしたことを報告する鷹野。
prompt.prompt_jp: パソコンが インターネットを___ました。
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the verb Takano actually (comically mis-)uses.

feedback.correct_en: The joke is that Takano personifies the PC as having 'quit' the internet — やめる. The humor depends on this un-tech word choice. 切る or 閉じる would be more normal IT verbs and would kill the gag.
feedback.incorrect_en: 切る or 閉じる are what a tech-literate speaker would say, but Takano's IT vocabulary gap is the whole point of the scene.

contrast_examples.jp: パソコンがネットをやめた。

prompt.context_jp: 鷹野の作業効率を評する語り。
prompt.prompt_jp: 鷹野の作業効率だけは常に底を___ていた。
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the verb that completes the idiom '底を〜 = scraping bottom'.

feedback.correct_en: 底を這う ('crawling along the bottom') is the fixed metaphor for sustained lowest-level performance. 歩く or 走る don't collocate with 底を in this sense.
feedback.incorrect_en: 歩く / 走る would be literal motion verbs that don't evoke the stagnation metaphor the narrator wants.

contrast_examples.jp: 株価が底を這っている。
contrast_examples.en: The stock price is scraping bottom.
He is walking on the road. (literal)

prompt.context_jp: 鵜飼が服を貸してくれた鵙尾に大仰に礼を言う場面。
prompt.prompt_jp: 鵙尾さん ご協力いただき 心より感謝___まする 行こう。
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the verb that completes this exaggeratedly formal thanks.

feedback.correct_en: 感謝申し上げる is the keigo set phrase for 'I offer my gratitude'. Ukai is being theatrically polite (even using 〜まする) because thanking Mogio pains her pride.
feedback.incorrect_en: 言わせる / 思う don't form a keigo expression of thanks; they'd break the archaic-polite register Ukai is deliberately laying on thick.

contrast_examples.jp: 心より感謝申し上げます。

prompt.context_jp: 鵙尾と鵜飼の言い合いが終わる場面。
prompt.prompt_jp: 鵙尾はふっと___の力を抜き、鷹野の顔を覗き込んで、柔らかい声で話しかけた。
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the body part in the idiom 'to relax, drop one's tension'.

feedback.correct_en: 肩の力を抜く is the standard idiom for 'relax / let go of tension'. Shoulders are where Japanese locates built-up stress.
feedback.incorrect_en: 手の力を抜く is literal (relaxing one's grip); 頭の力を抜く is not an idiom. Neither captures the overall de-escalation Mogio shows here.

contrast_examples.jp: 肩の力を抜いて話そう。

prompt.context_jp: 機嫌が悪い鵜飼が後輩に対して言う。
prompt.prompt_jp: 用件があるなら 10秒で___ろ。
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the blunt verb (imperative) Ukai uses.

feedback.correct_en: 伝える fits 'convey/get your message across in 10 seconds' — curt, task-focused, matching her irritated mood. 話す is softer and more open-ended; 聞く would mean 'listen', which flips the direction.
feedback.incorrect_en: 話せ would soften the demand to 'speak'; 聞け ('listen') reverses who is doing what. Ukai wants the junior to deliver content fast.

contrast_examples.en: Could you talk to me a bit? (soft)

prompt.context_jp: 鶸田が「雉谷さんと営業に行かないと」と言ったのに対する雉谷。
prompt.prompt_jp: いいよ こっち___ 俺 やっとくから。
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the particle+pronoun fragment that fits 'as for my side'.

feedback.correct_en: こっちは contrasts 'my side' with Hiwada's — Kijitani is saying 'as for things over here, I'll handle them'. The contrastive は carries the reassurance.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would introduce 'my side' as a new subject rather than contrasting it against Takano's call; を doesn't fit the slot grammatically.

contrast_examples.en: This side is the tough one. (identifying)

prompt.context_jp: 鵜飼が鶸田の同行を渋々認める場面。原文は『いても いなくても かまわないけど ジャマだけは しないで』。
prompt.prompt_en: Which line sounds most like curt, exasperated Ukai telling Hiwada he can tag along?

choices.text: いても いなくても かまわないけど ジャマだけは しないで
いらっしゃってもいらっしゃらなくても構いませんが、お邪魔なさらないでください
来ても来なくてもいいから邪魔しないで欲しいんだけど

feedback.correct_en: A keeps Ukai's blunt, slightly impatient tone with だけは and the imperative-like しないで — matching her 'I don't care, just stay out of the way' attitude.
feedback.incorrect_en: B is over-polite keigo that doesn't fit her character. C is grammatical but sounds whiny/explanatory rather than clipped and commanding.

contrast_examples.jp: ジャマだけはしないで。
contrast_examples.en: Just don't get in the way. (clipped, firm)

contrast_examples.jp: お邪魔なさらないでください。

prompt.context_jp: 鵜飼が同期の鵙尾に服を貸してほしいと頼む場面(原文は『ウチの鷹野に似合いそうな服 貸していただけませんでしょうか？』)。
prompt.prompt_en: Which phrasing matches Ukai's deliberately over-humble request to her peer?

choices.text: ウチの鷹野に似合いそうな服 貸していただけませんでしょうか？
鷹野に似合いそうな服、貸してくんない？

feedback.correct_en: A piles on humble/polite forms (〜ていただけませんでしょうか) which creates the comic 'eating crow' effect — proud Ukai forcing herself into keigo with a peer. B is too casual for the moment; C is a flat command and wouldn't persuade Mogio.
feedback.incorrect_en: B/C destroy the humor: part of the joke is that Ukai is painfully polite with someone she'd normally snap at.

contrast_examples.jp: 貸していただけませんでしょうか。
contrast_examples.en: Might I possibly have you lend it? (very humble)

prompt.context_jp: 鷹野がIT苦手かと聞かれて答える場面(原文は『ITは 私のことが苦手なようです』)。
prompt.prompt_en: Which line best captures Takano's signature deadpan reversal joke?

choices.text: ITは 私のことが苦手なようです
私はITが苦手なようです
ITの私への苦手意識があるようです

feedback.correct_en: A inverts the expected 'I'm bad at IT' into 'IT seems to be bad at me', which is the whole joke. B is grammatical but completely ordinary; C is awkward and loses the punch.
feedback.incorrect_en: B says the obvious thing and misses the humor. C is a stilted paraphrase that doesn't sound like a punchline.

contrast_examples.jp: ITは私のことが苦手なようです。
contrast_examples.en: IT seems to dislike me. (joke inversion)

prompt.context_jp: 鵜飼と鵙尾の言い合いを止めなくていいかと聞かれた鳩山の答え(原文は『ああ いつものことだから』)。
prompt.prompt_en: Which reply best fits laid-back Hatoyama waving off concern?

choices.text: ああ いつものことだから
はい、こちらでは日常茶飯事でございますので
いつもだよ、いつも、いつも！

feedback.correct_en: A is relaxed and reassuring — a senior who's seen it all brushing it off. B is absurdly formal for this casual office aside; C is theatrically repetitive and doesn't match Hatoyama's calm style.
feedback.incorrect_en: B treats a quick coworker aside like a client meeting. C would make Hatoyama sound flustered, which he never is in this chapter.

contrast_examples.jp: 日常茶飯事でございます。

prompt.context_jp: 鷹野がボランティアをしているかもという話を聞いた鵜飼の反応(原文は『彼女のお給料は 我々が必死で 稼いだお金ってことです』)。
prompt.prompt_en: Which phrasing most naturally conveys Ukai's bitter 'our hard-earned money' complaint?

choices.text: 彼女のお給料は 我々が必死で 稼いだお金ってことです
彼女のお給料は、我々が必死に稼いだお金なのです
彼女の給料というものは、我々の労働の対価の一部に相当するわけです

feedback.correct_en: A uses 〜ってことです, the spoken 'that means…' summary that fits Ukai's venting among colleagues. B is grammatical but stiffer; C is bureaucratic and would feel out of place in heated breakroom talk.
feedback.incorrect_en: B/C are too formal/written for a frustrated colleague monologuing. ってことです is exactly the spoken register she's in.

contrast_examples.jp: つまり損してるってことです。
contrast_examples.en: So it means we're losing out. (spoken)

contrast_examples.jp: つまり損失が生じているのです。
contrast_examples.en: In other words, losses are being incurred. (written/formal)
